messages.subject: Re: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
messages.subject_clean: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Dear Eric,

I just came to know from one colleague that DISTANCE doesn't work in
mountain topography. I am really frustrated at this last minute. But,
according to Marques and Buckland (2004), Marques et al. (2007), Strindberg,
Buckland and Thomas (2004), I am still believe that good survey design (with
automated survey design engine) and inclusion of covariates might work to
estimate group density of Assamese macaque in mountain topography of Nepal.
Could you please suggest me as early as possible? I am worrying too much
that if it doesn't work, I have to leave this project which is really
frustrating!

Sincerely,
Ganga

Hi Ganga=2CThere is nothing preventing you from designing a good survey for=
 any geographic area. =20
In this paper by Len Thomas=2C we had a geographically complex study area. =
 We couldn't afford to sample every fjord=2C so we divided the area up into=
 32 manageable-sized pieces in GIS=2C and randomly sampled 5 of them.  We u=
sed Distance to design good=2C design-unbiased surveys for each of those ar=
eas.  The design is described here:
http://www.marinemammal.org/mmru/williams/thomas%20williams%20sandilands%20=
jcrm%20survey%20design%202007.pdf
and the analysis of the resulting survey data is described here:http://www.=
marinemammal.org/mmru/williams/williams%20thomas%20jcrm%202007%20015-028.pd= <http://marinemammal.org/mmru/williams/williams%20thomas%20jcrm%202007%20015-028.pd=>
f
You'd have to "flatten" your 3D study area in GIS into some 2D shapefiles=
=2C but the automated survey design algorithms in Distance work fine in com=
plex areas.  The amount of survey effort you can conduct is a function of l=
ogistics and funding=3B not of the algorithms that Distance can handle.  I =
don't know what you mean by the use of covariates=2C but it sounds like you=
 have some issues you need to work out at the design stage (e.g.=2C having =
a steep versus a flat stratum=2C or bare rock/vegetation stratum).  It's go=
od to sort these out at the design stage=2C rather than relying on unnecess=
arily complex analyses later on. =20
Good luck=2CRob

messages.body_plain:
The only reason why mountain topography causes problems is that it can
be impossible to traverse randomly-positioned lines, so that a random
design may need to be compromised to some degree.  It is better to work
with flat projections of all distances and areas.  So line length is the
length of the line on a 2D map, distances of detected animals from the
line are horizontal distances, and the size of the study area is its
area on a 2D map.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
messages.subject_clean: Discussion about the automated survey design, GIS and MCDS
messages.body_plain:
If it is difficult to traverse random lines, then a point transect
option can work well in many circumstances, e.g. birds that typically do
not show much reaction to the observer.  If you rely on flushing animals
to detect them, then point transect sampling will not work, as you are
likely to flush those near the point before reaching it.

Typically, you can expect lower precision for the same effort when you
use point transects instead of line transects, so usually, the option
would only be used where it is impractical to use line transect
sampling, or where it is believed that the assumptions are easier to
satisfy when surveying from points rather than lines.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: field size and edge effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

My name is Justin and I'm starting new project looking at the effects of =
different management practices on grassland birds.  I would like to use d=
istance sampling in my bird surveys but I have a few concerns.  The field=
s I'll be working in are relatively small and irregular shaped for the mo=
st part (not square or rectangular).  My smallest fields could only be 6h=
a and my largest around 16ha.  I'm concerned with my number of detections=
 per species and was considering pooling across management type (8 fields=
 per management type).  Because the fields are so small and the edge effe=
cts would be so great, would using distance sampling be worth it?  It see=
ms like my analysis could get really complicated due to all the edge conc=
erns whether I did point surveys or line transects.  From my reading it s=
eems like edge effect could be handled with the help of GIS.  I appreciat=
ed any guidance and information you can provide.  I need to get this iron=
ed out before this field season.  Thanks for your time.

Cheers,
Justin

messages.subject: Re: field size and edge effects
messages.body_plain:
Justin, you don't clarify whether you can position points anywhere, or=20
whether they can only be placed at field edges.  If you can position=20
them anywhere, then a systematic grid of points placed at random over=20
your study area should largely deal with edge effects (i.e. you can=20
ignore them, and just do a standard analysis), if the edge effects are=20
primarily due to birds being at higher density in the edge habitat.  If=20
for example many of your fields were surrounded by a different habitat,=20
then you can extend the grid of points into the next habitat to avoid=20
edge effects - see section 7.2.1 of the 2004 adv distance sampling book.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: determining when data qualify as clusters
messages.subject_clean: determining when data qualify as clusters
messages.body_plain:
Sharon, the decision has nothing whatsoever to do with what proportion
of your observations is of birds in clusters.  If the clusters are
well-defined aggregations of birds, then the better option is to analyse
as clusters, even if 99% of your observations are of single birds.
However, the methods are extremely robust to which option you choose to
do - if you analyse both ways, you are likely to get very similar
results.  Model selection can be more problematic though if you analyse
clusters as if they were separate individuals all at the same distance -
this causes overdispersion in your data.  I haven't checked back, but my
suggestion to analyse a cluster of 6 as 6 separate individuals all at
the same distance might have been because distances were grouped, and
someone had recorded 6 birds in one distance interval as if they were a
cluster when they weren't.  Or it might have been because clusters were
loose, poorly defined groupings, in which case it is likely to be better
to record each bird and its distance from the point separately.
Analysing clusters as individuals is also a trick for dealing with size
bias - allowing for the fact that your data are typically biased towards
the larger, more detectable clusters - see the intro DS book for a
discussion of this issue.

Steve Buckland

On 24/02/2011 22:34, Sharon wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I want to clarify how to determine whether a data set should be analyzed as "individual obs" or "clusters."
> >
> > I am preparing to analyze point count data collected during the breeding season, of birds (primarily songbirds). For most species, the majority of observations were of single individuals. However, for many species there were observations of multiple individuals (ranging from 2-20), reported together at a **single distance.**
> >
> > My thought is that for single species, these data comprise mostly of observations of single individuals, and would NOT be analysed as clusters. However, if true, how do I handle the situation where 5 individuals were seen at "distance X" (e.g. 25m away)? Do those 5 individuals get entered as 5 separate rows of data (ie, 5 single observations each at 25m)? What if 25% of the observations were of 2-5 individuals, the rest were of single individuals.
> >
> > The "Intro to Distance Sampling" book by Buckland et al states on p. 164 "If point transects are used for objects that are sometimes recorded in clusters during the survey period, the recording unit should be the cluster, not the individual object, and analyses should be based on clusters." That would seem to argue for my analyzing my data as clusters, even though there is a preponderance of single individuals observed.
> >
> > On the contrary, in reviewing the archives for this listserve I found a response to Johanna's posting around June 7 2010. The recommendation was to analyze these data as "individual" {"If 6 individuals are in a group record as 6 individual distances"). Was S. Buckland thinking these individuals could be recorded all at the **same** distance?
> >
> > I think the bottom line is, at what point does a data set become one reflecting clusters?  Once 50% of my observations are of>1 individual? Or 75%? Or if 50% of my observations are more than 5 inviduals? 10 indviduals? I am just throwing out hypothetical numbers here to demonstrate my lack of clarity on this issue.
